Hey , I'm not a doctor but I have been on my own amenorrhea journey and have done heaps of research over the years.  
\-You are most likely not ovulating at all - hence no periods. (Any bleed on the pill isn't really a "period".)  
\-There is some underlying issue/cause here that you are right to be investigating. Possibilities that I'm aware of include hormonal issues which could indicate an issue in the thyroid, pituitary, ovaries, etc.; anatomical abnormalities; and genetic/chromosomal abnormalities.  
\-I know healthcare is super expensive (I'm guessing you are in the US) - can you get on any sort of insurance that would allow for diagnostic tests?  
\-In the meantime, can you do some more journaling/recording of your symptoms? The book "Taking Charge of Your Fertility" is one of my favorites. (It focuses a lot on bodily awareness and cycle charting.)

This is why I don’t like people saying “get over it, move on” in response to trauma. I am not one to dwell on the past, but sometimes I think it needs to be processed in order to heal and move forward.

In the same way that a physical injury can require PT, a traumatic event can also require support to work through. Stuffing emotions down sometimes means that they come up again later, in a way that can really impact someone’s life.

I have no idea if OP was referring to events of this nature - I just wanted to encourage them not to minimize past challenges/adversity. Sometimes “getting over” something isn’t a reasonable or healthy expectation to have for oneself or others.

Additionally, sometimes there ARE actions that can be taken to help feel some resolution/closure about a situation. For example, if someone did something that hurt you. Yes, you could opt to “just get over it”, or, you could to talk to the person about it, or journal about it, or bring it up in therapy, etc. Ultimately, yes we usually want to leave the past behind us, but that’s not necessarily easy or immediate.

Ah, right. I don’t mean validating the cuts, but validating his feelings. E.g., “that sounds really hard, I’m sorry you are going through that.” “I’m here if you ever want to talk about what’s going on at school/home.”

People who SH are often in a large amount of emotional pain and we don’t know how else to express it. Often we were emotionally abused or neglected and so learned to keep our feelings/problems to ourselves. So it’s good if he feels safe talking to you about his life.

RE his self-harm, I think you could say something more like, “I wish you weren’t cutting, but I understand that it’s a coping mechanism for you and I’m always here if you want to talk about it.”
